title: Reading 1 John

objectives.can: Read 1 John continuously, following its argument through its repeated contrasts.

explanation.summary: 1 John is written in the same plain Greek as the Gospel of John, but it does not tell a story. It argues, by setting one thing against another, and by saying the same few things again in new words. If you can follow the contrasts, you can follow the letter.

sections.heading: Contrasts in pairs
body: The letter is built on opposites. The first is light and darkness: ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν καὶ σκοτία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδεμία (1 John 1:5), where the negative οὐκ … οὐδεμία restates the positive. The second is love and hatred, in 2:9–11. The same sentence shape is used for both sides.

In 2:10 and 2:11 the two halves are set side by side: ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ …, and then ὁ δὲ μισῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ …. δέ marks the turn. When you meet one half of a pair, expect the other half to follow in the same grammatical shape.

sections.heading: ὁ λέγων, ὁ ἀγαπῶν, ὁ μισῶν
body: The letter likes to describe a person by an article with a participle: 'the one who says', 'the one who loves', 'the one who hates'. You met this as the substantive participle. In 2:4 the pattern is ὁ λέγων ὅτι Ἔγνωκα αὐτὸν … ψεύστης ἐστίν: the participle gives the person, the ὅτι clause gives what the person claims, and the predicate gives the author's verdict on the claim.
When a single article governs two participles joined by καί, as in 2:9 (ὁ λέγων … καὶ … μισῶν), a single person is described by both.

sections.heading: ἐάν and the subjunctive
body: The letter uses condition after condition. In 1:6, 1:8 and 1:10, ἐὰν εἴπωμεν ὅτι … begins three sentences in a row, each followed by a verdict. In 1:9 the pattern is turned round: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν …. In 2:3 the condition comes last: ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ τηρῶμεν.

All of these are ἐάν with the subjunctive, in the first person plural, 'if we …'. Treat each as a general condition about 'us'. A related form is the indefinite relative with ἂν and the subjunctive: ὃς δ’ ἂν τηρῇ in 2:5, 'whoever keeps'.

sections.heading: The perfect tense
body: 1 John uses the perfect often, as in ἐγνώκαμεν (2:3) and Ἔγνωκα (2:4), from γινώσκω, and in τετελείωται (2:5). Grammarians describe the perfect as expressing a present state that results from an earlier action. With γινώσκω, the perfect ἔγνωκα is often best translated by the English present 'I know', since 'to have come to know' is 'to know'. Do not turn every perfect into 'have' + past participle in English; read what state is claimed.
The letter also repeats formulas. ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι … ('by this we know that …') occurs in 2:3 and 2:5. Once you recognise the formula, the rest of the sentence is easy to find.

sections.heading: Old and new, said twice
body: Repetition and variation carry the thought. In 2:7–8 the author writes ἐντολὴν καινήν and ἐντολὴν παλαιάν, and then ἐντολὴν καινὴν again with πάλιν. The same word returns with a different adjective. Read these as deliberate: the word is the same, the point is the contrast.

misunderstandings: Reading a perfect as a simple past. ἐγνώκαμεν is not 'we knew' (that would be an aorist) but a state: 'we have come to know' or 'we know'.
Assuming that every ὅτι means 'because'. After λέγων or γινώσκομεν it introduces what is said or known, as in 2:4 and 2:5.
Taking the three ἐάν clauses of 1:6, 1:8 and 1:10 as one. Each has its own verdict, and each begins afresh.
Treating ὁ λέγων as a verb. It is a participle with an article, a noun phrase: 'the one who says'.

deeper.heading: Why 1 John is hard to outline
body: Readers have never agreed on a neat outline of the letter, because the same themes of light, love and knowing keep returning in new forms. Some describe the structure as a spiral rather than a line. The grammar does not decide the question; it shows only that the author argues by repeating and varying his sentence patterns.

examples.analysis: After ὅτι, two clauses joined by καί: ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν, and σκοτία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδεμία. The first states the claim, and the second states it again by denying the opposite. οὐδεμία strengthens the negative: no darkness at all.

examples.analysis: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν is ἐάν with a present subjunctive, first person plural: 'if we confess'. The main clause is πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος, with a ἵνα clause after it. The conditional pattern of 1:6–10 is the backbone of the passage.

examples.analysis: ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι is one of the letter's formulas. After ὅτι comes the perfect ἐγνώκαμεν, 'we have come to know' or 'we know'. The ἐάν clause at the end, ἐὰν … τηρῶμεν, states the test of that knowledge.

examples.analysis: ὁ λέγων is a substantive participle, the subject. The ὅτι clause gives its words: Ἔγνωκα αὐτόν, a perfect. Then μὴ τηρῶν, another participle, continues the subject, and ψεύστης ἐστίν is the predicate: the person is called a liar. μή (not οὐ) is the usual negative with a participle in the New Testament, and here it fits a participle that describes a type of person.

examples.analysis: ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ is a substantive participle with its object. ἐν τῷ φωτὶ μένει is the verb with its location. Compare 2:11: ὁ δὲ μισῶν … ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστίν. The two verses have the same shape with opposite content.

options: A single past event with no present result: 'we knew'
A present state resulting from earlier action: 'we have come to know' or 'we know'
A repeated habit in the past
check.explain: The perfect gives a state that holds now. That is why the clause is a test applied now: ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν …

options: No one; the sentence is only a question
Two persons, one who says it and one who hates
One person, who both says it and hates his brother
check.explain: One article, ὁ, governs both participles, which καί links. The verb ἐστίν (word 14) is singular and the subject is one person.

options: ὁ μισῶν: the one who hates
check.explain: ἡ σκοτία is the nominative. τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ is accusative, the object. ὅτι gives the reason for the one who hates not knowing where he is going.

reading.why: Nine verses that contain the letter's formulas (ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν), its perfects, its ἐάν-conditions, its substantive participles and both of its great contrasts, light and darkness, love and hatred.
